title: Independent Pharmacy GLP-1 Aftercare Studios
one_liner: A turnkey cash-pay aftercare membership that gives independent pharmacies their first PBM-free service line.
customer: Independent community pharmacies (~17k in the US). One report has ~41% not dispensing obesity GLP-1s in Q4 2025 over poor reimbursement.
problem: Insiders assume Walmart, CVS and Amazon win GLP-1 care because of scale. Independents get squeezed by PBM reimbursement below cost and skip the category, even though they see patients monthly and pharmacists can check dose, side effects and nutrition.
solution: A 'studio' kit: leased body-composition scale, a protocol (dose-step check, protein and strength plan, red-flag triage), scheduling and billing for a $39-59/month cash membership, and links to pill and vial cash-pay fulfillment. Includes collaborative-practice documents and, where state law allows pharmacist prescribing, protocols for it. Monthly outcomes report to the pharmacist and to referral partners.
why_now: $149-$299 cash pills remove the need for dispensing margin to justify the category. Lilly and Novo cash channels route through retail pharmacies. Big chains launched their own pharmacist support programs in 2026, so independents need a counter-offer.
revenue_model: $199-399/month SaaS per pharmacy plus 20% of membership revenue, plus device lease.
non_obvious_insight: GLP-1 is the first drug category where a pharmacy can earn from services with zero PBM exposure. Independent pharmacists are more trusted locally than a chain's app and have a natural monthly touchpoint.
first_30_days: Partner with one state pharmacy association or wholesaler buying group. Pilot in 5 pharmacies at $49/month. Track retention and a muscle proxy (grip and chair-stand) for the first cohort.

title: Inverter-Telemetry Credit Bureau for African Solar
one_liner: Turn the cloud data that hybrid inverters and batteries already stream into a consented energy cash-flow score, so lenders, insurers and installers can finance an asset boom that official statistics cannot see.
customer: Solar and battery asset financiers, MFIs and banks in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, plus installers who need financing to close sales. Insurers and DFIs paying for verified performance come later.
problem: Africa installs 17 GW of solar in 2026 (+45%), 75% of the growth is distributed, and it imports more battery dollars than panels. Ember says its estimates are 2x official figures and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data, so credit bureaus and insurers have nothing to price on. Installers cannot get customers financed, and lenders cannot see collateral health or borrower activity.
solution: With owner consent gathered through the installer, pull production, load, battery health, uptime and location data from inverter and BMS clouds (Victron VRM, Solarman for Deye, Growatt, Huawei, Solis). Compute diesel displacement and savings, a load-profile proxy for business activity (cold-room cycles, salon hours), collateral health and tamper flags, and installer quality scores. Sell an API and dashboard to lenders, with remote-lock hooks and insurer feeds as add-ons.
why_now: Distributed solar plus batteries has become private infrastructure. Stationary packs fell 45% to about $70/kWh, African equity funding is concentrated while debt replaces equity (so lenders need collateral visibility), and India's UPI fee change shows how fragile transaction-data underwriting is. The US also needs neutral telemetry, since Sunrun and Tesla's 16.8 GW capacity-as-a-service has no disclosed verification standard.
revenue_model: $2-6 per scored asset per month or per-report fees, a 1-2% origination fee on financing it unlocks, installer SaaS, insurer data licensing, and later verification fees from results-based financing programs.
non_obvious_insight: The best alternative-credit dataset in Africa is already being emitted by hardware nobody thinks of as a bureau. Energy consumption is a real-time proxy for small-business activity, and the inverter is both the collateral and the sensor. Because the data layer is vendor-neutral, it can later certify firm distributed capacity for utilities and hyperscalers, something Tesla and Enphase cannot credibly do for each other's fleets.
first_30_days: Integrate two APIs (Victron VRM and Solarman/Deye) and sign 3 installers in Lagos, Nairobi or Johannesburg with 300+ systems between them. Collect customer consents through the installers' apps and publish a free installed-base map. Take the top-scoring 30 customers to one MFI or asset financier for a pilot loan pool, charging a 2% origination fee.

title: Exoskeleton Hike Rentals for Active Older Adults
one_liner: Trailhead rental hubs and guided exo-hikes that let 60-80 year-olds keep climbing with powered hip assist.
customer: Active adults 55+ (pay $70-120 per day), outdoor retailers and outfitters, senior-living activity directors and trail-gateway towns.
problem: Consumer exoskeletons now exist ($900-2,300, with the leader's models at about $2,000-2,300) but buyers hesitate to spend that on something they have never tried, and older hikers quietly stop hiking as knees and hips fade.
solution: A rental fleet with fitting, safety briefing and waivers, guided group hikes, retailer rental corners, and monthly exo-walks for senior living communities. Renters get a credit toward purchase and we earn affiliate commissions.
why_now: Consumer hip-assist exoskeletons reached the $900-2,300 range with heavy marketing, the leading brand is pushing an 'offline' era with retail and rental hubs, and the active-older-adult demographic is driving the category.
revenue_model: $79 per day rentals, $30 per person guided add-ons, 8-12 percent affiliate on purchases, retail rental-program fees and $1-2k per month senior-living contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is trial, not price, and manufacturers lack local operators; a small team can own the try-before-you-buy channel. The real work is waivers, fitting and injury protocols, which are also the moat.
first_30_days: Buy or borrow four units (about $8k), set up demo weekends at one or two outdoor shops or campgrounds near a popular trail, run a senior-center exo-walk, and start charging rentals from week two.

title: Narrow Networks and Reference Pricing for Pet Insurers
one_liner: Pet insurers reimburse whatever clinics invoice while losing about 10 points a year to price/mix inflation; build the pet-insurance 'PPO' from affordable-care clinics whose invoices run about 44% lower.
customer: Mid-size pet insurers and MGAs (payers), affordable-care and team-based independent clinics (network), and insured owners steered by a lower deductible or higher reimbursement in-network.
problem: 2025 premiums grew about 19.7% against 9% growth in insured animals, and insurers do not contract with clinics, so they have no lever on price. Owners face renewal shock. Corporate chains (Mars about 2,100 clinics; GoodVets going from 75 to 116) are bound to margin targets and are unlikely to cut price.
solution: Contract a metro-by-metro network of independent affordable-care clinics with agreed fee schedules, standardized service coding and direct pay. The insurer offers an in-network tier (for example, 90% reimbursement with no deductible on routine lines). We provide claims routing, spectrum-of-care quality guardrails, and network-savings reporting. Start with one metro.
why_now: The premium/enrollment gap is now visible in trade press, roll-ups are accelerating, and the affordable-care model is documented at $130 vs $233 average invoices. Model-law adoption is pushing insurers toward transparency and cost containment.
revenue_model: Shared savings (20-30% of verified savings vs a market baseline) or 3-5% administration fee on network claims. Clinics pay nothing.
non_obvious_insight: 'Reimburse at any vet' is sold as a feature, but in human health the equivalent indemnity design gave way to networks once cost trend outran wages. Steering is the only demand-side lever pet insurance has not pulled, and the low-priced independent tier is spare capacity waiting for volume.
first_30_days: Identify 15-20 team-based or low-cost independents in one metro. Get an NDA with one small insurer or MGA and pull 200 claims. Reprice them against the network fee schedule to show projected savings (target 15% or more). Propose a 6-month shared-savings pilot on an existing product tier.

title: Ruling-Backed Tariff Engineering for Product Brands
one_liner: A productized design-and-ruling service that helps mid-market brands legitimately re-spec products across tariff-line boundaries and locks the result in with a CBP binding ruling.
customer: Mid-market consumer and industrial product brands with $10-100M in revenue and at least $1-2M in annual duty spend: footwear, bags, apparel accessories, home goods, hardware, e-bike and powersports parts, and other products with metal components.
problem: Adjacent tariff lines can differ by tens of percentage points, and the 2025-26 regime made the gaps bigger. Section 232 metals lists keep expanding and being recalibrated, and copper smelt-and-cast reporting started July 30, 2026. Yet brokers are asked for a classification only after the tooling is cut and the design is frozen. Product teams never learn that a small change in materials, construction, packaging or set composition can legally change the line. Importers also avoid asking CBP for rulings, assuming it is slow or risky.
solution: Sell two steps. First, a fixed-fee HTS boundary audit: map the top SKUs to the classification tests, spec thresholds and comparable public CBP rulings that determine the line, and list the small design or packaging changes that would legitimately move each one. Second, an engineering sprint with the supplier that documents the changed product and files a CBP binding ruling request under 19 CFR Part 177. The deliverable is a ruling letter, which is a lasting shield for reasonable-care defense. Add a ruling-watch subscription that alerts brands when CBP issues a ruling on competitor or adjacent products.
why_now: The IEEPA reversal shifted the burden to product-specific tariffs (Section 232 and 301) where design details matter. The July 2026 copper reporting and the rewritten 232 valuation rules make product composition a compliance and cost variable. Brands are in a rare window when rate spreads are large enough that redesign pays for itself in one production run.
revenue_model: $4,500 boundary audit for five SKUs; $18-35k per engineering sprint including ruling preparation and filing; optional success fee of about 10% of first-year duty savings, capped. Ruling-watch subscription of $500-$2,000 a month.
non_obvious_insight: Classification turns on physical facts of the article as imported, and those facts are set by designers, not brokers. The most valuable document in a tariff war is a dull letter from CBP's ruling office, and requests cost nothing to file. Tariff engineering is legal when the product really changes, and it requires evidence, which is where a broker's habit of documenting everything matters. Trade lawyers do this ad hoc for large clients, but nobody packages it for mid-market brands at design stage.
first_30_days: Pick two verticals with high design freedom and large rate spreads. Use public CBP rulings to build a boundary map for a prospect's own top SKU as a free sample. Cold-email 40 product, sourcing and COO leads at $10-100M brands with their own sample map. Sell three $4,500 boundary audits and use them to select the first ruling filings. Sign a trade lawyer as reviewing counsel on the ruling requests.

title: Renewal Radar for Silent AI Exclusions
one_liner: Track carriers' filed AI exclusions and tell brokers, 90 days before renewal, which clients just lost AI coverage, then place the affirmative buy-back.
customer: Independent agencies and regional brokers (10-200 staff) with commercial books, their E&O carriers, and MGAs.
problem: Since January 2026 ISO-style generative-AI endorsements (CG 40 47 and CG 40 48) and far broader carrier forms, such as W. R. Berkley's 'absolute' AI exclusion, are attached at renewal, often buried. Clients use AI in ways they never disclosed. Brokers carry E&O exposure for failing to warn, and no tool maps which of a broker's 300 clients face AI exclusions or what AI each client actually uses.
solution: A rate and form filing scraper (public SERFF filing access) plus an endorsement parser that normalises exclusion breadth: gen-AI only versus any AI, bodily injury versus advertising injury, vendor-supplied AI. It feeds a renewal calendar imported from agency-management CSVs. A 12-question client AI-use questionnaire, optionally backed by an SSO or expense-report scan for AI tools. Output is a one-page 'AI coverage gap letter' plus a list of affirmative AI markets for placement.
why_now: 1 Jan 2027 renewals are the first big cycle after the Verisk endorsements became available, and AIG, Great American and Berkley filings landed through 2026. Affirmative AI capacity now exists (Armilla via Lloyd's, AIUC, Munich Re aiSure), so a gap and its fix can be sold together.
revenue_model: $250-800 per month per agency, $150-600 per gap letter for non-subscribers, 10-15% commission on affirmative cover placed, and $2-5k per month filing-intelligence subscriptions for MGAs and carriers.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is triggered by their own E&O fear, not curiosity about AI. The filings are public but unreadable, so the moat is a normalised exclusion database nobody at a brokerage has time to build. Silent AI cuts both ways: an unexcluded policy is a reason to ask for affirmative cover, so the gap letter also works as a sales tool for the broker.
first_30_days: Scrape SERFF filings in five large states and build the tracker. Start a free weekly 'AI exclusion tracker' newsletter aimed at 500 brokers. Offer 10 agencies a $500 concierge gap audit on their five biggest accounts. Sign one affirmative-AI MGA for placement referrals.

title: CAM and Insurance Pass-Through Audits for Micro-Tenants
one_liner: Read a small tenant's lease, recompute the landlord's annual reconciliation, and dispute overcharges inside the audit window, on contingency.
customer: Restaurants, salons, clinics, gyms and boutiques on NNN or modified-gross leases in strip centers and small retail, typically 1,000-5,000 sq ft.
problem: Landlord reconciliations of common-area, tax and insurance charges are opaque, and pass-throughs rose with property insurance and tax bills (prior knowledge). Audit rights exist in the lease but expire in weeks or months, and owners never read the lease. Rising costs are the top financial challenge for small firms.
solution: Upload the lease and reconciliation. An LLM extracts audit rights, caps, exclusions, gross-up, base year, admin fees and pro-rata share, recomputes the statement, drafts the audit request or dispute letter, calendars deadlines, and escalates to an auditor partner for contested items. Add a renewal-negotiation packet.
why_now: Long-context models read leases cheaply. Enterprise tenants have lease-audit firms, but micro-tenants were never worth the hourly rate.
revenue_model: 25-30% of amounts recovered, with a $99 flat triage fee for leases that show no error.
non_obvious_insight: The lever is the deadline, not the arithmetic. Most owners have never seen their own audit clause, and landlords count on that.
first_30_days: Collect 10 leases and reconciliations through a restaurant association or business improvement district. Run manual audits, measure the hit rate, sign the first contingency deals and refine the extraction.

title: Medicare-First Longevity Kit for Independent Practices
one_liner: Longevity medicine built on what Medicare already pays for, sold as a workflow kit to independent primary-care practices.
customer: Independent primary-care and DPC-adjacent practices (2-15 clinicians) with 500-2,000 Medicare patients each.
problem: The longevity boom (Function $2.5B, Neko ~$7B, Superpower up to $349/yr) targets cash-paying under-55s, while the highest-risk group, seniors, has a covered prevention stack that is badly under-used. Well under half of beneficiaries take the Annual Wellness Visit, and independents lack the workflow to turn covered services into a healthspan program.
solution: A configurable 'healthspan AWV' template with functional tests (chair-stand, grip, gait speed), cognitive and falls screens, covered lipid, diabetes and bone screening, and vaccine gap-closing. A monthly care-management billing layer (APCM codes introduced in 2025). Compliant ABN-based cash upsells for ApoB or Lp(a). Practices get scripts, patient handouts and a collections dashboard.
why_now: APCM monthly primary-care codes are new (2025). The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge began Jul 1, 2026, pulling seniors into metabolic care. Cash longevity prices keep rising, which cedes the 65+ segment. About 82% of doctors are employed, so the remaining independents are underserved by digital vendors.
revenue_model: $600-1,200/month SaaS per practice plus 15-20% of incremental collected revenue (est. $30-80k per clinician per year of newly captured billing).
non_obvious_insight: 'Longevity' for the 65+ is mostly a billing-and-workflow problem on already-covered benefits. Founders build for cash because that is where the venture buzz is, and they overlook the biggest and sickest demographic, whose payer is already at the table.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 independent practices via state IPAs and DPC-Medicare communities. Offer a free 30-day audit of their AWV and care-management capture, pulled from claims, showing dollars left on the table. Convert to a $499/month pilot with a success fee.

title: Shared Emergency Desk for Autonomous Fleets
one_liner: A neutral 24/7 first-responder interface (hotline, dispatch API, geofence directives) that small AV, robot-truck and delivery-robot operators rent instead of building.
customer: Newer and second-tier AV operators (autonomous trucking, shuttles, delivery pods, robotaxi entrants), and city and county 911 dispatch centers on the public-facing side.
problem: Regulators are asking for a human phone number, not more autonomy. NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on July 8, 2026, and California's AV enforcement rules take effect in 2026 (as I understand them). Waymo alone runs about 70 remote agents per shift from two centers in the Philippines, which small operators cannot copy.
solution: A US-staffed desk trained on fire and police protocols. It offers standardized emergency-response guides, one API through which dispatch centers can stop, unlock or reroute any subscribing fleet, compliance logs, and drills for first responders.
why_now: Driverless trucking is commercial (Aurora about 200 trucks, Gatik 85k driverless orders, Einride listed), new AV entrants are launching, and states are writing rules. Compliance deadlines land in 2026.
revenue_model: $500-2,000 per vehicle per year or an $8-25k monthly fleet retainer, plus training contracts with cities.
non_obvious_insight: A commodity BPO with liability attached scales with vehicle count, and neutrality is a feature because cities prefer one interface for all fleets. Large operators build their own desks, so the long tail of new entrants is the market.
first_30_days: Interview 10 safety and compliance leads at autonomous trucking and delivery-robot companies. Build a minimal hotline plus web console for a single pilot, co-design the protocol with 2 city or county dispatch centers, and sign 2 paid pilots at about $5k a month.

title: Care-First Reverse Mortgages With Locked Payouts
one_liner: A care-planning broker that funds long-term care from home equity and releases the money only to verified caregivers and facilities.
customer: Homeowners 70-85 with $300k+ equity and thin liquid savings, or their adult children holding a power of attorney. The channel is elder-law attorneys, geriatric care managers and hospital discharge planners.
problem: Long-term-care insurance is failing policyholders: Genworth has about $31.8B of approved premium hikes, and 2023 hikes averaged 51%. Care runs $75-115k a year, and Medicaid retrenchment is coming. The one big asset is home equity, but advisors still treat reverse mortgages as a last resort and lump sums invite fraud and sibling fights.
solution: Start with a 12-month care budget and plan. Match it to a reverse-mortgage line of credit (HECM or proprietary), through an NMLS-licensed broker or a co-brokering partner. Then open a care wallet: funds go only to vetted payees (agency, facility, or a family caregiver under a documented personal-care agreement with payroll), with a ledger for siblings and Medicaid look-back records, and multi-party approval for any other outflow.
why_now: Proprietary reverse mortgages now hold 52% share against 48% for HECM, so products are better. Seniors hold $14.92T in home equity. LTC insurance is unravelling, the 80+ cohort is exploding, and elder fraud hit $7.7B in 2025 (up 59%), which makes lump-sum liquidity risky without controls.
revenue_model: Broker origination compensation on funded loans, roughly 1-2% of loan amount, plus a $49 a month care-wallet fee. Licensing the wallet to lenders as a fraud-protection differentiator is later upside.
non_obvious_insight: The product isn't the loan; it's controlled disbursement plus a care plan. Reverse mortgages are viewed with suspicion because of how the cash gets spent, and a locked, audited payout stream fixes the exact failure mode that ruined the category's reputation.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed reverse-mortgage broker, publish 'how to pay for care with home equity' content, and build referral relationships with 10 elder-law firms and care managers. Loans close in about 60-75 days, so first revenue lands inside six months.

title: The Master's Letter Apprenticeships
one_liner: Six-week, premium apprenticeships with master craftspeople that give teens the one credential AI cannot counterfeit: a named human's signed, callable letter about what they actually did.
customer: Affluent parents of 15-18 year olds (private-school and college-admissions-anxious) paying $6-12k per placement. Masters (luthiers, boat-builders, stone masons, pastry chefs, bookbinders, restoration carpenters, farriers) get 60% of tuition.
problem: Application essays are AI-contaminated, and admissions offices are shifting to in-person writing, short answers, and interviews because they can't trust take-home work. Wealthy families are hunting for hard-to-fake, embodied, verifiable experiences. Meanwhile master craftspeople in aging trades lack apprentices and income to take them on.
solution: A curated roster of about 40 masters per metro. Structured 6-week apprenticeships on real work, not shadowing. Each ends in a finished object with the maker's mark and a Master's Letter written to a rubric, backed by a recorded interview and a verification page colleges can call. An alumni network and independent counselors' referral fees drive supply of students.
why_now: Admissions officers openly discount take-home writing and are moving to formats that are harder to fake. Entry-level white-collar hiring is shrinking (Stanford payroll data show early-career workers in AI-exposed jobs losing ground), which raises the prestige and perceived safety of craft. Aging masters have shops and no successors.
revenue_model: 25-40% platform fee on $6-12k tuition. Corporate- or foundation-sponsored scholarship seats. $900 'Family Master Day' add-ons.
non_obvious_insight: The product isn't the skill. It is a third-party attested effort signed by a reputationally exposed human. A letter from a master who stakes their name is the analog of the old handwritten recommendation, now scarce. The supply side is an underused asset: elderly masters with empty workbenches.
first_30_days: Recruit 8 masters in one city through trade guilds. Publish a landing page. Recruit 5-10 independent college counselors as referral partners at 10%. Sell 12 slots for summer 2027 starting in the winter admissions-anxiety season. Get background checks and liability insurance in place.

title: School Deepfake-Nude Incident Response Retainer
one_liner: A 24/7 retainer that walks school districts through the first 72 hours of an AI-generated nude incident: hash-based takedowns, evidence handling, reporting duties and parent communications.
customer: School districts, charter networks and independent schools. Channel: school risk pools, cyber and liability insurers and brokers.
problem: Nudify apps let anyone turn a student photo into sexual imagery. Schools improvise: staff viewing the images can itself be illegal, mandated-reporting and Title IX duties are unclear, and takedowns must be filed on many platforms. The federal TAKE IT DOWN Act (2025) requires platforms to remove reported intimate imagery within 48 hours, with platform compliance due May 2026 (from memory), but victims and schools don't know the process.
solution: A playbook plus tooling: secure intake that hashes images without staff viewing them (StopNCII and NCMEC Take It Down style), pre-filled takedown requests, a state-by-state legal duty checklist, evidence logs, communication templates for parents and students, and counselor referral. A retained hotline handles live incidents.
why_now: The TAKE IT DOWN Act's platform obligations kicked in this year, incidents are proliferating, and insurers are re-underwriting districts for cyber and child-safety exposure.
revenue_model: $3-12k annual retainer per district, per-incident fees, and bundle or referral deals with insurers and school risk pools.
non_obvious_insight: The worst thing a school can do is look at the evidence, so the product is a don't-look-just-hash workflow. Insurers are the channel because one mishandled incident costs far more than the retainer.
first_30_days: Draft the playbook with a school-law attorney and a former juvenile detective. Pitch 3 school-insurance brokers or state school-board risk pools. Run free tabletop exercises for 5 districts. Convert the best relationship into the first paid retainer.

title: Executor-of-Last-Resort for Solo Agers
one_liner: A subscription that names a licensed fiduciary as your executor and runs daily wellness checks, so a childless retiree isn't found weeks late and handed to a court-appointed stranger.
customer: Unpartnered or childless adults 65+ with $100K-$1.5M estates (too small for most corporate trustees, too large to ignore), plus their elder-law attorneys, senior living communities and Area Agencies on Aging.
problem: Solo agers have no obvious executor, agent or emergency contact, and named friends or nieces often flake. Japan shows the downstream effect: 37,227 people living alone were found dead at home in H1 2024, nearly 4,000 undiscovered for over a month. The US has no equivalent service layer, and intestate estates go to public administrators.
solution: A 'Stewardship Plan'. (a) A licensed professional fiduciary or trust company partner agrees to serve as successor agent and executor. (b) Passive wellness signals (phone, smart speaker, utility use, optional wearable) plus a daily automated or human check-in escalate to neighbors and welfare checks. (c) A digital go-bag holds accounts, medications, pets, keys and funeral wishes. (d) At death it triggers funeral instructions, securing the house, clear-out and estate administration for a fee schedule.
why_now: Cheap ambient signals and voice-AI check-in calls make monitoring inexpensive. Death care is proving roll-up-able (Everstory, SCI), yet no one serves the years before death for people without heirs. Estates and consolidator data show volume is flat, so services attached to existing customers are where growth sits.
revenue_model: $39-$79/month subscription, executor fees at death (often statutory, a few percent of the estate), margin on clear-out and estate services, and B2B fees from senior living and AAAs.
non_obvious_insight: The first customer isn't dying. She is buying certainty that someone competent shows up on the worst day. Subscriptions fund the acquisition of a low-cost executor book that pays out later.
first_30_days: Partner with a licensed fiduciary in one state. Sign 3 elder-law attorneys. Recruit a 30-person waitlist through senior centers and 'elder orphan' groups. Charge $99 setup plus $49/month and run the daily check-in calls manually at first.

title: Tariff Refund Recovery for Downstream Buyers
one_liner: Importers of record are collecting over $100B in tariff refunds, but the small businesses that paid tariff surcharges on their invoices are owed a share and nobody is collecting it for them.
customer: Mid-size US contractors, restaurant groups, retailers and manufacturers ($5M-$200M revenue) whose 2025-26 supplier invoices carried explicit tariff surcharges or tariff-attributed price increases.
problem: Refunds go to the importer of record, and many importers already passed the cost through. Downstream buyers may have contract or unjust-enrichment claims, but their AP teams never tracked surcharges. Small importers also find filing costly ('not without a cost,' Colorado Sun, 2026-07-02), so cash sits with parties who have no incentive to share it.
solution: Connect to QuickBooks, NetSuite or the AP inbox and extract every invoice line mentioning a tariff or surcharge. Map each vendor to its importer of record using public import records. Estimate the refund-attributable share and generate demand packets with contract citations. A partner law firm handles escalations on contingency. Default settlement is a vendor credit memo, which preserves the relationship.
why_now: More than $100B has been refunded (CNBC 2026-08-07, Forbes 2026-09-09), the government is fighting an order to refund all importers (WaPo 2026-08-11), tariff lawsuits are surging, and 25 states are challenging the replacement Section 122 tariffs. That means a second wave of surcharges to track.
revenue_model: 20-30% contingency on recovered cash or credits. After the first recovery, $299-$999 per month SaaS to track surcharges and refund clauses on future tariff swings.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is watching who receives the refund, and nobody watches who funded it. Many invoices literally say 'tariff surcharge, pass-through.' Vendors prefer credit memos to cash, so recoveries can be quiet and relationship-safe. The same invoice-clause tooling becomes a permanent tariff-swing shield.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 SMBs through trade associations and small-business communities and pull 24 months of AP exports. Run the analysis by hand with a lawyer's template letter and produce a $1M aggregate identified-claim demo. Sign two contingent agreements and send the first ten demand letters.

title: 72-Hour Diligence Engine for Vet Clinic Acquirers
one_liner: Upload a PIMS export and P&L and get retention cohorts, price-versus-volume decomposition and doctor-dependence risk in three days, then keep the same schema as the post-close KPI dashboard.
customer: Mid-size vet groups, search-fund and PE platforms buying 5-50 clinics a year, and practice lenders.
problem: Roll-ups are continuing (GoodVets buying WellHaven, 40+ hospitals), but small acquirers rely on broker packages and QuickBooks. PIMS exports differ by system, and price increases can hide falling active-client counts, a real risk given visits reportedly down three years.
solution: Ingest PIMS exports across major systems, normalize service lines, then compute cohort retention, active clients, revenue per DVM and tech utilization, price/mix/volume decomposition, discount and controlled-substance anomalies, and revenue at risk if the owner-vet leaves. Output a quality-of-earnings-lite memo, then continue as a post-merger KPI dashboard.
why_now: M&A pace is high, buyers include newer and smaller platforms without in-house analytics, and LLMs make messy export mapping cheap. Incumbents such as IDEXX are buying workflow AI (CoVet), not diligence tooling.
revenue_model: $3-6K per target for diligence, $1-2K per clinic per month for post-close dashboards.
non_obvious_insight: The price hikes that flatter EBITDA may be masking client attrition. Diligence that sees through price versus volume is worth far more than its fee, and brokers will not build it because it works against their headline numbers.
first_30_days: Approach 10 mid-size groups and search funds with a free retrospective on one closed deal. Build export mappers for 3 major PIMS. Sell 3 paid diligences at $3K each.

title: Outside-Processing Milk Run for Job Shops
one_liner: Scheduled pickup routes and batching software for the heat-treat, plating and anodize bottleneck behind reshored machining.
customer: 10-100 person machine shops and fabricators, plus special-process houses (heat treat, anodize, plating, passivation, paint) that want fuller batches.
problem: As machining orders rise (machinery jobs +6.1k in August, record capital-goods orders), the constraint moves downstream to special processes. Shops ship parts by carrier ad hoc, parts sit in queues, and paperwork gets lost. ISM supplier deliveries have slowed for eight straight months. Environmental cost and owner retirements limit new special-process capacity (my inference).
solution: Vans on fixed weekly or daily routes between shops and vetted process vendors. Batching gives vendors full loads. Barcode chain of custody carries cert paperwork (heat-treat charts, NADCAP status). A promised turnaround (for example 5 days) is tracked by software.
why_now: Reshoring in existing walls raises job counts while outside-process capacity has not grown. Slowing deliveries make lead time visible.
revenue_model: Per-stop fee plus 8-12% margin on outside-processing volume. Vendor SaaS. Later, acquire a heat-treat or anodize house.
non_obvious_insight: Outside processing often accounts for most of a job's elapsed lead time but only a small share of touch time. That bottleneck yields to logistics and batching, not new furnaces, and adding a van is cheaper than adding an oven.
first_30_days: Pick one region such as Grand Rapids, Greenville or Wichita. Interview 20 shops. Sign two heat-treat or anodize houses. Run a one-van pilot two days a week and charge per stop.

title: Thermal Commons on Failed Golf Courses
one_liner: Turn shuttered golf courses into shared geothermal borefields that heat and cool the neighborhoods that already surround them.
customer: Gas and electric utilities running thermal-energy-network pilots, housing authorities and multifamily or 55+ community owners next to a course, and the course owner as a land-lease seller.
problem: Networked geothermal works, but it is starved for land. Dense neighborhoods have no room for borefields, so pilots dig up streets or use scraps of parking lots. Meanwhile ~90 golf courses close a year, leaving 100-150 acre owners stuck in expensive rezoning fights with neighbors who hate new housing.
solution: A small developer that (1) screens closed and for-sale courses by distance to heat loads (apartments, schools, 55+ communities) and utility franchise, (2) options the best sites, (3) runs thermal response tests, (4) designs a borefield and neighborhood loop, and (5) sells capacity to the utility or thermal service to buildings under long contracts. The surface stays green as a public park or trails, which turns a NIMBY fight into an amenity and speeds approvals.
why_now: Utility pilots are real and funded. Eversource's Framingham phase 2 has a $7.8M DOE grant with construction in 2026 and launch in early 2027. NYSEG's UTEN pilot in Ithaca and National Grid's Massachusetts approvals add to that. State thermal-network mandates are spreading, and the utility model is still being written, so a site-finder-and-developer has room to define it.
revenue_model: Phase 1 (first six months): paid feasibility and site-screening reports for utilities, cities and housing authorities ($25-80k each, often grant-funded) plus land option fees. Phase 2: own or co-own the borefield asset with availability payments from a utility, or per-building thermal service contracts over 20 years.
non_obvious_insight: Land, not technology, is the bottleneck, and a failed golf course arrives pre-cleared, flat, surrounded by customers and owned by someone losing money. A borefield leaves the surface untouched, so the same acreage can also be the park that gets you the permit. The pitch to a utility is 'we bring you a community-approved site, not a science project'.
first_30_days: Build a GIS screen of ~500 closed or listed courses against multifamily density and utility service areas in states with thermal-network programs (NY, MA, CO, MD, MN, WA). Send data packs on the top 10 sites to utility pilot teams and housing authorities. Land one paid feasibility study and sign two cheap options ($5-20k each).

title: Grant Recovery Desk for Small Cities
one_liner: A contingency-fee grant compliance and reimbursement service for small cities receiving FEMA, DOJ and counter-drone money with no staff to document it.
customer: Towns and counties with populations of 5-100K, especially those receiving disaster reimbursements and new safety grants (for example the $500M FEMA counter-UAS program).
problem: Small governments lose federal reimbursements to incomplete documentation, procurement missteps and audit findings. With federal agencies shrinking and reorganizations stalled in court, help is thinner. Dallas County is cutting IT staff, and local budgets are tight.
solution: A software-plus-service program that structures the grant lifecycle: eligibility check, procurement compliance, receipt capture, quarterly reporting and closeout audit packages. It uses AI to read award terms and flag non-compliant purchases before they happen. Paid from recovered funds.
why_now: New grant streams (counter-drone, cyber, disaster) are landing at localities while federal grant-management staff are being cut. Regulators enforce documentation harder as budgets tighten.
revenue_model: Contingency of 4-8% of recovered or protected award dollars, with a minimum retainer. A city with $2M in awards yields about $80-160K.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer pays nothing up front, and the alternative is losing money already awarded. Contingency pricing turns a dreaded compliance cost into free money for a small clerk's office.
first_30_days: Offer free award-file reviews to 10 small cities identified from public award lists. Build a compliance checklist per program. Sign 2 contingency deals.

title: Heat-Health Desk for Medicare Advantage Plans
one_liner: Forecast-triggered outreach and cooling delivery for the heat-vulnerable members whose hospital bills the health plan pays.
customer: Medicare Advantage, D-SNP and Medicaid managed-care plans in the Southwest, Southeast and Pacific Northwest (supplemental-benefits and medical-director teams).
problem: Summer 2026 brought the hottest US July on record and a European heatwave with about 38,000 provisional deaths (secondary source). Heat waves drive ER visits and admissions among older, medicated, low-income members. Plans pay the downstream cost but do not know which members lack working cooling or live on top floors. Cooling supplemental benefits are underused.
solution: Risk-stratify members by housing type, utility arrears, medications that impair heat tolerance and prior heat visits. Trigger phone outreach ahead of forecast heat, deliver and install AC or fans through partners, run check-in calls on days 1-3, and help prevent utility shutoffs. Report avoided ER visits.
why_now: After the 2026 heat shock, plan medical directors are looking for concrete heat programs. Off-season (Oct-Feb) is when supplemental-benefit budgets get set.
revenue_model: Per targeted member per month in season, or per intervention, plus shared savings.
non_obvious_insight: The party that absorbs the cost of heat is the health plan, not the city. Heat is a claims-management problem and belongs in the plan's budget.
first_30_days: Use public hospital heat-visit data to build a cost-per-heat-day case. Pitch 5 regional plans for a 2,000-member pilot next season, and line up an AC-delivery and check-in vendor.

title: Gig Social-Security Compliance Engine for Mid-Size Platforms
one_liner: A four-week compliance package for India's long tail of aggregator platforms that cannot build labour-code tooling in-house.
customer: Indian home-services, logistics, ride and staffing platforms with 5k-100k gig workers.
problem: India's labour codes require aggregator contributions to a social security fund and worker registration. Over 20% of gig workers log 70+ hours a week, and the government forced platforms to drop 10-minute branding in Jan 2026. Founders bear the audit exposure.
solution: e-Shram registration sync, contribution computation, hours-worked flags and worker benefit statements. The wedge is a fixed-fee readiness audit and setup for logistics and home-service platforms.
why_now: Labour codes are now in force, enforcement is starting, and quick-commerce attrition (51% at Zepto) pushes platforms to show worker-welfare records.
revenue_model: Rs 10-30 per worker per month plus a setup fee.
non_obvious_insight: Large platforms build in-house. The 500 mid-size platforms cannot, and they have real budgets because penalties land on founders.
first_30_days: Run free readiness audits for 10 platforms and refine the contribution calculation with a labour-law firm partner.

title: Import Compliance Desk for Hobby Brands
one_liner: Subscription compliance for small tabletop, designer-toy, card-accessory and collectible brands covering CPSC eFiling, product certificates, EU representative and tariff classification.
customer: Indie designer-toy studios, board-game and miniature publishers, Kickstarter creators and card-accessory brands importing from Asia or selling into the EU and UK, with $0.5M-$20M in revenue.
problem: CPSC electronic certificate filing for regulated imports became mandatory on 8 July 2026 (no value-based exemption; foreign-trade-zone entries follow 8 Jan 2027). The EU requires a responsible person for consumer products. De minimis ended in Aug 2025, so small parcels are dutiable. Hobby brands have no compliance staff, and blind-box and collectible toys straddle the children's-product line.
solution: Per-SKU compliance dossiers (accredited lab test-report management, certificate generation, filing data handed to brokers), classification lookups, an EU authorized-representative service, label review, and a landed-cost API for the brand's storefront.
why_now: eFiling is live, counterfeit-toy seizures show heightened customs attention, and crowdfunded creators are hitting duty surprises for the first time.
revenue_model: $199-999/month plus $150-500 per-SKU dossier fees and an EU representative fee.
non_obvious_insight: Hobby brands do not hire compliance, and backers forgive late delivery but not a customs seizure. Vertical-specific rulings (dice, sleeves, miniatures, plush) are reusable across every customer, which is what makes a generic compliance vendor less useful.
first_30_days: Sell a $299 eFiling readiness audit to 15 publishers via BoardGameGeek and Kickstarter creator communities. Partner with one customs broker and one accredited lab.

title: Time-to-First-Part: Install Readiness for Machine Dealers
one_liner: A pre-delivery site-scan and commissioning package that gets backlogged machines cutting parts weeks sooner.
customer: Machine-tool, laser and robot dealers and OEM sales teams, plus 20-200 employee manufacturers buying their first big machine.
problem: Unfilled capital-goods orders sit at $953B after a record $85.9B in July orders. Much of it lands in old buildings with no as-built drawings. Machines arrive to floors, doors, crane paths and utility drops that cannot take them, so crated $500k machines sit idle. Dealers often get paid only at acceptance.
solution: A 20-minute phone or LiDAR walkthrough becomes an as-built model. Software checks the machine footprint, door and aisle clearance and rigging path, flags slab and vibration issues (with a ground-penetrating-radar partner), lists air, coolant and chip-handling needs, and produces a rigging plan and punch list. It can also dispatch vetted riggers and millwrights.
why_now: Reshoring is happening inside existing walls, the equipment backlog is at a record, and riggers and millwrights are scarce. Phone-based 3D capture (LiDAR, Gaussian splats) has matured.
revenue_model: $1.2-3k per site package, paid by the dealer or bundled into the machine price. 10-15% referral on rigging. Dealer team subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: Dealers get paid at acceptance, so time-to-first-part is their cash-flow metric and they will pay to shorten it. The unfilled-order backlog hides a second backlog of installed-but-not-producing machines.
first_30_days: Sign three regional dealers (CNC, laser or robot) for a pilot. Do 10 scans with iPhones. Produce a sample report. Measure install days saved against comparable installs.

title: Disordered-Eating Tripwire for GLP-1 Prescribers
one_liner: A cheap, documented eating-disorder screen and escalation network embedded in GLP-1 telehealth intake.
customer: White-label medical groups that supply prescribers to many telehealth brands, GLP-1 telehealths, med spas and their malpractice carriers.
problem: GLP-1 use was ~50% among binge-eating-disorder patients and ~42% among atypical anorexia patients (JAMA Psychiatry 2026), and an NEJM 2026 perspective warned about masking and worsening disordered eating in telehealth. An investigation tied four white-label medical groups to ~30% of telehealth firms receiving FDA warning letters, and MDL 3094 has 4,700+ cases pending. Plaintiff lawyers and boards look for the next vector, and no screening or monitoring layer exists.
solution: A 3-minute validated screen (SCOFF or EDE-Q short form) inside intake, 2-question monthly check-ins, rules-based escalation to a network of ED-trained dietitians and therapists, and an exportable audit trail for boards and insurers.
why_now: FDA sent 30 letters in Mar 2026 and 25 in Jun 2026. Regulators, boards and carriers are moving to documented safeguards. The data showing high GLP-1 use in eating-disorder populations is new in 2026.
revenue_model: $3-6 per screened patient, $40-80 per escalation (paid by the prescriber or referral network), and a malpractice-carrier discount program.
non_obvious_insight: In white-label telehealth, liability concentrates in the medical group that sits behind dozens of brands, so a cheap, documented safeguard is standard-of-care insurance. ED providers also need referral flow, so escalation pays for itself.
first_30_days: Pitch two mid-size white-label groups or a 20k-patient telehealth. Deliver via an embeddable link, run 500 screens, and publish flag-rate benchmarks. Recruit 10 ED-trained clinicians for escalation.

title: Pay Farmers to Under-Irrigate, Not Fallow
one_liner: A broker and satellite-verification layer that pays growers of alfalfa, hay and cotton for mid-season deficit irrigation and hands corporate and municipal buyers audited acre-feet.
customer: Buyers: corporate water coalitions (Amazon put $20M into the Water Resilience Coalition's Colorado River effort, $32M raised toward a $100M goal) and Lower Basin cities and water agencies. Sellers: irrigation districts and forage/annual-crop growers. The buyer pays.
problem: The 2027-2036 Colorado River framework pushes cuts onto agriculture (about 70% of the river), yet corporate money has no settlement layer. Fallowing is politically toxic and guts farm income. Drip and efficiency upgrades often do not reduce consumptive use, so nobody can say what a verified acre-foot is.
solution: A standard split-season contract. The grower skips the last irrigation cycles, or accepts deficit irrigation at pre-agreed growth stages. Consumptive use is measured by satellite ET (an OpenET-style ensemble) against a five-year baseline and paired control fields. Payment is escrowed per verified acre-foot, and the buyer gets a basin-and-year-tagged certificate. Wedge product: one district pilot plus a buyer dashboard. Federal credit is not needed to start, so begin with districts that already hold Reclamation conservation agreements.
why_now: The Aug 2026 Record of Decision fixed the 2027-2036 rules. Powell plus Mead storage is about 36% of capacity, the lowest since before Glen Canyon Dam filled. Corporate money is arriving, and open ET datasets are now good enough to audit individual fields.
revenue_model: 10-15% spread on each acre-foot transaction (roughly $40-90 on a $400-600/af price), plus $20-50k/yr verification SaaS to districts.
non_obvious_insight: Only cuts in consumptive use create basin-level savings, and forage crops tolerate a mid-season deficit far better than farm economies tolerate fallowed fields. Buyers are really paying for measurement certainty, so whoever owns the audit trail sets the price and the standard.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: run retrospective ET for 10 alfalfa/hay growers in one Lower Basin or Grand Valley district (public data, free tier) and price the acre-feet they could offer. Days 10-25: build a one-page buyer pitch and dashboard mock. Days 25-30: pitch the Water Resilience Coalition and two city water agencies to underwrite a 500-1,000 af pilot for the 2027 season, since contracts get negotiated over winter.

title: AI-Guided Feline Heart Screening by Technicians
one_liner: Handheld ultrasound with AI probe guidance lets technicians capture heart clips on cats, with remote cardiologist over-read making HCM screening a routine add-on instead of a referral.
customer: General-practice clinics (senior and pre-anesthetic cats), breeders of at-risk breeds, and shelters; later insurers.
problem: Feline hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is common and often silent until clot or heart failure. Screening needs a cardiologist's echo, which is scarce and costs a few hundred dollars, so most cats are never screened. Cat households are growing (53M) and the vet workforce is not.
solution: Existing vet-priced handheld probes, a guidance app that prompts standard views and rejects poor clips (trained on cardiologist-labeled data), and a board-certified over-read within 24 hours with next-step recommendations. Sold as a 'senior cat heart check' and a breeder program.
why_now: AI acquisition guidance for novices has been proven in human echo, handheld ultrasound is cheap, vision models are strong, and remote reading is a way to stretch scarce cardiologists while techs take on more scope.
revenue_model: $60-90 per over-read, probe leasing at about $199 per month, and breeder program fees.
non_obvious_insight: The product is not AI diagnosis; it is AI acquisition guidance so a technician can collect usable images. The scarce resource is the cardiologist's time, so pooling over-reads creates the leverage, and the resulting longitudinal dataset improves guidance and screening protocols.
first_30_days: Sign 1-2 board-certified cardiologists on a per-read basis. Equip 5 clinics with handheld probes and run 100 screening scans. Measure the share of diagnostic-quality clips, then sell a $99 senior cat heart check.
